say: You give it a diagram where a line crosses two lines. It finds the unknown angle and **names the theorem** that justifies it.
Theorem 5: when a line crosses two lines, **corresponding angles** are equal exactly when the two lines are parallel.
what.in: two parallel lines cut by a third

how.higher: At Higher level it is a step inside a longer proof: in 2021 it gives the parallel line in the 20-mark proof that similar triangles have proportional sides.
how.ordinary: At Ordinary level it is a reason inside bigger geometry questions on Paper 2 (2015 and 2025), not a part of its own.

example.question: The lines $l$ and $m$ are parallel. A third line crosses them. The corresponding angles are $(4x + 10)^\circ$ on $l$ and $(6x - 20)^\circ$ on $m$. Find $x$ and the size of each angle. Give a reason.

steps.title: Spot the corresponding angles
steps.say: The two angles sit in the same position, one at each line. They are **corresponding angles**. $\hl{1}{(4x+10)^\circ}$ is on $l$ and $\hl{2}{(6x-20)^\circ}$ is on $m$.

lines.text: The lines are parallel, so Theorem 5 says they are equal.

steps.title: Make them equal
steps.say: Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel. Set $\hl{1}{4x+10}$ equal to $\hl{2}{6x-20}$.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Collect the $x$ terms on one side and the numbers on the other.

steps.title: Find the angle
steps.say: Put $x = 15$ into either angle. Check with the other.

ordinary.tip: Give a reason with each value. A value with its reason scores higher than a bare value.

say: You give it a triangle with two equal sides, or two equal angles. It finds the unknown angle and **names the theorem** that justifies it.
Theorem 2: in an isosceles triangle the two **base angles** are equal, and the other way round.

how.higher: At Higher level it is a step inside circle questions on Paper 2: in 2022 the isosceles triangle gives a 45° angle in a 10-mark part, and it appears again in 2025.
how.ordinary: At Ordinary level it is the main skill in three Paper 2 parts (2019, 2022, 2023), usually as a step in an angle-finding part worth 5 or 10 marks.

example.question: In the triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$. The base angles are $|\angle ABC| = (2x + 10)^\circ$ and $|\angle ACB| = (4x - 20)^\circ$. Find $x$ and $|\angle BAC|$. Give a reason.

steps.title: Find the base angles
steps.say: $|AB| = |AC|$, so the triangle is isosceles. The base angles are the ones opposite the equal sides: $\hl{1}{|\angle ABC|}$ and $\hl{2}{|\angle ACB|}$.

lines.text: Reason: isosceles triangle (Theorem 2), base angles are equal.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Collect the $x$ terms on one side and the numbers on the other.

steps.title: Find the angle at A
steps.say: Each base angle is $2(15) + 10 = 40^\circ$. The three angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$.

say: You give it a triangle with one side extended. It finds the unknown angle and **names the theorem** that justifies it.
Theorem 6: the **exterior angle** of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.

how.ordinary: At Ordinary level it was used once, in 2015: a 20-mark part where the value of $z$ comes from an exterior angle, with a reason required.

example.question: In the triangle $ABC$, the side $[BC]$ is extended to $D$. $|\angle BAC| = (2x + 10)^\circ$, $|\angle ABC| = 40^\circ$ and the exterior angle is $|\angle ACD| = (5x - 10)^\circ$. Find $x$ and $|\angle ACD|$. Give a reason.

steps.title: Pick out the angles
steps.say: The exterior angle is $\hl{1}{|\angle ACD|}$. The two interior opposite angles are $\hl{2}{|\angle BAC|}$ and $|\angle ABC|$, the ones not touching $C$.

lines.text: Reason: exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles (Theorem 6).

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.say: The exterior angle equals the sum of the other two. Write $\hl{1}{5x-10}$ equal to $\hl{2}{2x+10}$ plus $40$.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Tidy the right side, then collect the $x$ terms.

say: You give it a point or a shape and a transformation. It gives back the **image**.
A translation adds the same shift to every point. Central symmetry in the origin flips the sign of both coordinates.

how.ordinary: At Ordinary level it is the main skill in three Paper 2 parts (2018, 2019, 2022), a 5-mark translation inside a coordinate geometry question.

example.question: A translation maps $A(3, 5)$ to $A'(7, 2)$. (i) Find the image of $B(-1, 4)$ under the same translation. (ii) Find the image of that point under central symmetry in $(0, 0)$.

steps.title: Find the translation
steps.say: Compare $A$ with its image $A'$. The translation is the change in $\hl{1}{x}$ and the change in $\hl{2}{y}$.

steps.title: Translate B
steps.say: Apply the same shift to $B(-1, 4)$. Add $4$ to $x$ and $-3$ to $y$.

steps.title: Apply central symmetry
steps.say: Central symmetry in $(0, 0)$ changes the sign of both coordinates of $B'(3, 1)$.

ordinary.tip: Show the translation itself, as a shift in $x$ and in $y$ or on the diagram. It earns partial credit even if the answer is wrong.
Apply the same shift to every point. A correct shift applied to the wrong point still earns High Partial Credit.
Check the direction of the shift. An incorrect translation applied correctly still earns credit.
